question: Vinalopó University Hospital is the last privately managed public hospital operated by Ribera Salud in the Autonomous Community of Valencia. The contract – signed in 2007 by a representative of Ribera Salud, Pablo Gallart – should have come to an end in May 2025, with the hospital’s management returning to the public sector.

In 2024, however, the Valencian Government extended the contract to 2030, but failed to carry out the external audit required on quality of care and compliance with public service obligations. Internal company guidelines have also come to light that prioritise economic factors over patient rights, affecting thousands. 1.

Does the Commission believe that such practices, which could cause treatment to be denied or delayed for economic profitability reasons, are in line with the high level of protection for human health required by Article 168 TFEU?

Does the Commission believe that, in this case – in which no external audit was carried out and no prior call for tenders was made – the rules on reviewing and extending contracts established by Directive 2014/23/EU have been followed?
How does the Commission check that private-sector healthcare providers operating under public procurement contracts scrupulously comply with EU public health objectives?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.3.2026) The organisation and delivery of health services and medical care, including the management of health services and medical care, remain the responsibility of the Member States pursuant to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.

Where healthcare services are delivered under public procurement contracts or concessions falling within the scope of EU public procurement rules, Member States are responsible for ensuring compliance, including Directives 2014/23/EU and 2014/24/EU[1], as applicable.

Based on the elements available, it is not possible for the Commission to determine whether the arrangements concerning the Vinalopó University Hospital fall within the material scope of Directive 2014/23/EU or Directive 2014/24/EU.

Even if this was the case, national courts and review bodies laid down under the Directives on remedies in public procurement (Directive 89/665/EEC[2] and Directive 92/13/EEC[3]) are in the best position to assess, according to the facts of each case, whether contracting authorities and contracting entities have respected their obligations under EU law.
This reflects not only the system of remedies specific to EU public procurement law, but more broadly the system of judicial protection established by the Treaties.
